articles.title: Building a Charge Page Template for a Criminal Defense Site
articles.description: If you build or maintain a website for a criminal defense firm, most of your work will end up in one template: the charge page. A typical defense site has twenty to sixty of them, one for each offense the firm handles, sometimes split by county or by first and repeat offenses. They bring in most of the search traffic and most of the calls. A good charge page template makes those pages easy for lawyers and editors to write, consistent for readers and fast on a phone. A weak one turns every new page into a custom design job. This post covers how to design the template from the content model up, with notes from the kinds of problems that show up on real law firm sites. Start with a content model, not a layout Before opening a design tool, define the fields a charge page needs. Lawyers think in terms of the charge, the possible penalties, the court process and common defenses. The CMS should reflect that so editors fill in structured fields rather than one large rich text box. A starting model might look like this: charge_page: charge_name: string # "Domestic Battery" jurisdiction: string # state or county the page covers statute_refs: list # optional citations, plain text intro: richtext # first 80-120 words, answers "what now?" penalties: richtext # reviewed by a lawyer before publish process_steps: list # arrest, arraignment, hearings defenses: richtext faq: list[question, answer] attorney: reference # lawyer who handles these cases related_charges: list[reference] last_reviewed: date The last_reviewed field matters more than it looks. Penalties and procedures change, and a visible review date helps both readers and the firm keep pages accurate. Design the first screen for a phone Most people reach a charge page from a phone, often in a stressful moment. The first screen should show the charge name as the heading, a short opening that speaks to the reader's situation and a clear way to call. Large hero images push all of that below the fold, so keep them small or leave them out. A sticky call bar at the bottom of the viewport works well on mobile. Use a real tel: link, make the tap target at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels and test that the bar does not cover form fields or the cookie banner. Keep it out of the way on desktop, where a header button usually does the job. Build sections that editors cannot break Each field in the content model should map to a section component with fixed styling. Editors choose the content, not the fonts, colors or spacing. That keeps forty charge pages looking like one site rather than forty experiments. Some practical rules: Render the FAQ from the structured list so questions use consistent heading levels. Generate the related charges block from references, not hand-typed links, so renamed pages do not leave broken links behind. Show the attorney card from the referenced bio, including photo and name, so updates in one place flow to every page. Limit rich text options to headings, lists, links and paragraphs. Navigation matters as the number of charge pages grows. This guide on building a menu for a defense firm with many practice areas covers how to group charges so visitors and crawlers can find them. Keep it fast Charge pages compete in local search, and page experience is part of what Google considers. Watch the Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift. On law firm sites, the usual causes of trouble are oversized hero images, chat widgets that load early and block the main thread, and fonts or embeds that shift the layout as they load. Set explicit dimensions on images and embeds. Load third-party chat and tracking scripts after the main content. Self-host fonts or limit the number of weights. Test on a mid-range Android phone over a throttled connection rather than only on a fast laptop. Leave room for legal review and compliance Lawyers need to review penalty and process content before it goes live. Build a draft and review state into the CMS workflow, and record who approved each page. Attorney advertising rules vary by state, and some require disclaimers on certain pages. Add a disclaimer field or a site-wide component that can be switched on per page rather than hard-coding text. Accessibility belongs in the template too. Use proper heading order, sufficient color contrast and form labels that screen readers can announce. A person in crisis may be using assistive technology, and an inaccessible contact form loses calls. For more design ideas aimed at defense practices, see the collection of law firm website design guides. Questions developers ask about charge page templates Should each charge page have its own design? No. A shared template with structured fields keeps the site consistent and makes maintenance far easier. Variation should come from the content. How do I handle county-specific versions of the same charge? Use the same template with a jurisdiction field and require unique local content, such as the courthouse and local process, so the pages are not near-duplicates. Where should schema markup come from? Generate it from the structured fields so it stays in sync with the visible content. Only mark up what is actually on the page. SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense law firms, one firm per city. It helps them with website design, SEO for the charges they defend, visibility in AI search tools and SEO audits.

articles.title: Your Free Tier Is Not a Capacity Plan: Five Throughput Myths and a Concurrency Ramp
articles.description: A demo handles one request at a time. A launch sends ten at once. The endpoint falls over. Was the model worse today? Or did nobody measure the shape of the curve? I keep seeing the same five claims about free models and free servers. Each one sounds reasonable. Each one falls apart under a ten-minute test. I run these probes against MonkeyCode's free model access and its free server option while prototyping. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Nothing below depends on that relationship. Swap in any endpoint you control. The method is the point. Myth 1: "Latency grows linearly with concurrency" If one call takes two seconds, ten calls take twenty. Right? No. That is a queue, not a multiplier. Little's Law says concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by time in system. When arrivals outrun service capacity, waiting time stops being bounded. The curve has a knee. Left of it, latency is flat. Right of it, latency goes vertical and errors appear. You cannot read the knee in a doc page. You find it by ramping. Myth 2: "Retries add capacity" Retries feel like resilience. Under saturation they are a load multiplier. Say a third of calls fail and you retry twice. Offered load can nearly double. At the knee, that turns a brownout into an outage. A corrected model: retry only classified transient failures. Use exponential backoff with jitter. Keep a retry budget, something like ten percent of successful calls. Primary sources worth reading: AWS on backoff and jitter and the SRE book chapter on handling overload. Myth 3: "It is free, so the numbers do not matter" Free tiers make people skip measurement. "It is just a prototype." But the shape transfers. The knee moves. The existence of a knee does not. A prototype that dies at ten users teaches you nothing. A prototype with a written envelope teaches you where the queue belongs. Myth 4: "A 429 or a timeout means the service is broken" A 429 is admission control talking. It says your offered load exceeded what the server will accept. A timeout says your deadline was shorter than time to first byte. Neither one is a bug report. Both are signals to slow down, queue, or shed. Make 429 a first-class state in the client. Do not swallow it as an exception. Myth 5: "The model is the slow part" Can you prove that? Most people cannot. Split each request into a time budget: Client prep: serialize the prompt, sign the request. Connection: DNS, TCP, TLS. Time to first byte: queue wait plus prefill. Generation: first token to last token. Client parse: decode, validate, store. Without all five numbers, "the model is slow" is a guess with good manners. The artifact: a concurrency ramp Here is the probe. It is a template, not a run. I am not publishing numbers from it. Stop rule first. Stop a level when either condition fires: p95 exceeds three times the level-1 baseline. Error rate passes five percent. # ramp.py - template only. Point it at an endpoint you control. import asyncio, time import httpx URL = 'https://your-endpoint.example/v1/chat' LEVELS = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32] PER_LEVEL = 24 P95_STOP = 3.0 ERR_STOP = 0.05 async def call(client, sem, rows): async with sem: t0, ttfb = time.perf_counter(), None try: async with client.stream('POST', URL, json={'input': 'ping'}) as r: async for _ in r.aiter_bytes(): if ttfb is None: ttfb = time.perf_counter() except Exception as e: def summarize(rows, wall): lat = sorted((r['end'] - r['t0']) * 1000 for r in rows) q = lambda p: lat[min(len(lat) - 1, int(p * len(lat)))] errs = sum(1 for r in rows if not r['ok']) return {'rps': round(len(rows) / wall, 2), 'p50_ms': round(q(0.50)), 'p95_ms': round(q(0.95)), 'err': round(errs / len(rows), 3)} async def main(): async with httpx. AsyncClient(timeout=60) as client: base = None for level in LEVELS: sem, rows = asyncio. Semaphore(level), [] start = time.perf_counter() await asyncio.gather(*[call(client, sem, rows) for _ in range(PER_LEVEL)]) s = summarize(rows, time.perf_counter() - start) base = base or s['p95_ms'] print(level, s) if s['p95_ms'] > P95_STOP * base or s['err'] > ERR_STOP: print('stop: knee near level', level) break Reading the output Three fields matter more than the rest: rps tells you whether more concurrency bought throughput. p95_ms tells you where waiting started. err tells you where the server pushed back. If rps flattens while p95 climbs, you are past the knee. More concurrency is now just more waiting. The decision table Zone What you see What to do Left of the knee p95 flat, errors near zero Raise the cap slowly, keep the ramp in CI At the knee p95 jumps 2-3x Set your cap at half the knee Right of the knee p95 vertical, 429s or timeouts Queue, shed, or return a fast 503 No ramp at all no baseline You have no capacity envelope, only hope Half the knee, not the knee. Headroom is for the day your prompt gets longer. The gate you ship Now encode what you measured. Do not leave it in a notebook. # gate.py - cap below the knee you measured. import asyncio, random class Retryable(Exception): pass class Envelope: def __init__(self, knee, headroom=0.5): async def run(self, fn, *args, **kwargs): async with self.sem: for attempt in range(3): return await fn(*args, **kwargs) except Retryable: delay = (2 ** attempt) * 0.2 + random.random() * 0.2 await asyncio.sleep(delay) raise Retryable is yours to define. Map 429, 503, and connect timeouts to it. Map everything else to a hard failure. What this does not tell you The generator shares a network with the target. Measure from a second host when you can. TTFB mixes queue wait with prefill. The client cannot split them apart. A ramp is a snapshot. Provider-side changes move the knee without warning. One prompt shape is not all prompt shapes. Long prompts bend the curve down. Free tiers can change. That is a reason to re-run the ramp, not a reason to skip it. Who should not use this One-shot scripts and nightly batch jobs. Nobody is waiting on them. Teams with real load tests and SLO dashboards. Reuse those numbers instead. Anyone who cannot label synthetic traffic as synthetic. Ask first. So why ship a cap you never measured? You cannot defend a number you never took. Run one ramp. Write the knee in your README. If you are prototyping on a budget, run the same script against MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option before you commit to a paid plan. The script does not care whose endpoint answers.

articles.title: Measuring Calls and Forms Before A/B Testing a Law Firm Site
articles.description: If you build or maintain sites for criminal defense firms, someone will eventually ask you to "run an A/B test" on a charge page. Before you pick a tool, check whether the site can measure the thing the firm cares about. On most defense sites that is a phone call from a mobile visitor, and a surprising number of sites record it poorly or not at all. Testing without reliable conversion data produces confident charts about nothing. This post covers the measurement groundwork that should be in place first, with notes on the constraints that make legal sites different from ecommerce. Define the conversion with the firm, in writing Developers often default to whatever the analytics tool tracks automatically. For a defense firm that is the wrong starting point. Sit down with whoever runs intake and agree on what counts: A tap on a tel: link from a mobile device A completed contact or case review form A chat conversation that reaches a human, if the firm uses chat A call to a tracking number shown on the site Then agree on which of those count as primary. Many firms care far more about calls than forms. Write the definitions down, because six months later nobody will remember whether chat openings were included. Track tel: link taps and form submissions as events Google Optimize was shut down on September 30, 2023, so many teams now pair GA4 with a separate testing tool or run server-side experiments. Whatever you choose, the conversion events have to exist in analytics first. GA4 has a recommended event called generate_lead for form submissions. Phone taps need a custom event. A minimal version looks like this: Fire the form event only after the server confirms the submission. Firing on button click counts failed validations and double taps. Add a data attribute to each phone link so you can tell header taps from in-content taps, which matters when the test changes where the number appears. Never send what the visitor typed Google Analytics policies prohibit sending personally identifiable information, and a defense intake form collects some of the most sensitive data a website can hold: names, phone numbers, charges, arrest dates. None of it should reach analytics, a heat map tool or a session recorder. Check a few things before any test goes live. Form fields should be excluded or masked in any recording tool. URLs should not carry form values as query strings after submission. Event parameters should describe the form, never its contents. If the firm uses a third-party form service, confirm where submissions are stored and who can see them. Connect site events to calls the firm actually received A phone_tap event shows intent. It does not prove a call connected. Call tracking with dynamic number insertion can close that gap by showing a different number per source and logging calls on the provider's side. If you use it, keep the firm's main number consistent in the footer, schema markup and Google Business Profile so local search signals stay clean. The richest data lives in intake. A short field asking how the caller found the firm, plus a weekly export, lets you compare test variants on signed cases rather than raw contacts. For the form side of that work, designing an intake form a frightened caller will finish covers how many fields to ask for and how to word labels for a scared person typing on a phone. Size the test honestly Most defense charge pages see modest traffic and few conversions. Run the numbers before you promise a result. If a page produces twenty calls a month, a split test chasing a ten percent lift will take far longer than anyone will wait. With small numbers, test large changes to the first mobile screen, run variants for fixed periods and keep a change log in the repo. Before and after comparisons are weaker evidence than a true split, but they are often the only realistic option, and they are fine if you say so in the report. Keep every variant compliant Each variant is attorney advertising. If a test changes headlines, claims or disclaimers, the firm's lawyers need to approve it, and state bar advertising rules apply to every version a visitor might see. Build the approval step into your deployment process so a variant cannot ship by accident. More on testing ideas for legal sites is collected in the conversion testing library for law firm websites. Questions about conversion tracking on law firm sites Should phone taps count as conversions in GA4? Mark them as key events if the firm treats calls as its main goal. Report them separately from forms so changes in one do not hide changes in the other. Is a session recording tool safe on a defense site? Only with strict masking of every input and a review of where recordings are stored. Many firms decide the risk is not worth it. Which testing tool should I use? Pick one that works with your stack and supports server-side or flicker-free variants. The tool matters less than clean conversion data and an honest sample size. It builds websites for defense practices, handles SEO for the charges a firm defends, works on visibility in AI search tools and runs SEO audits.

articles.title: Claude config: rules and guardrails for Claude Code on .NET + Angular projects
articles.description: I work on .NET and Angular projects with Claude Code. For every new project I kept writing the same instructions again: which stack to use, how to handle Git, what Claude must never do on its own, how to ask questions. So I put all of it in one place: claude-config, a public template of rules plus a small Claude Code plugin. Repository: https://github.com/AngeloDotNet/claude-config What is in the repository Claude Code loads the files under .claude/rules/ by itself, so the rules are copied into each project and nothing is installed globally. The modules are: Module When it loads What it covers core.md always stack, tests, observability, Docker scope, interaction rules git.md branches and commits security.md authentication, secrets, input, CSP, supply chain, OWASP Top 10 2025 and ASVS 5.0 frontend.md when editing *.ts, *.html, *.css, *.scss Angular backend.md, backend-architecture.md, backend-app.md when editing C# or project files .NET docker.md Dockerfiles and Compose files containers Optional modules (email, infrastructure, feature workflow) live in .claude/rules-optional/ and are switched on only when a project needs them. The rules are written in Italian, because that is the language I work in, while code, identifiers and commit messages stay in English. You can change that to suit your own team. Rules that do most of the work A few of the rules in core.md shape almost every session: One question at a time. When Claude is unsure, it stops, asks a single question and waits for the answer before going on. It never bundles several questions together. Claude makes only local commits by default. It does not push, open pull requests, create tags or publish releases unless the project explicitly approves those operations in its CLAUDE.md, one operation at a time. Without that approval, they stay with the developer. Plan before substantial work. For features, non-trivial fixes and refactorings, Claude writes a plan file first, then executes it one step at a time, ticking each step only after build and tests. No trusting memory for fast-moving APIs. For libraries that change often, Claude checks the documentation of the installed version. Verify before declaring done. Build and tests run first, and any errors are reported as they are. The plugin: kit-config Written rules are only a suggestion, so the plugin turns the most important ones into hooks: a reminder of the one-question rule on every prompt; a check that allows only one question per AskUserQuestion call; a guard on shell commands that always blocks git init, forced pushes (git push --force and its variants), deleting remote branches, git reset --hard, git clean -f, --no-verify and forced recursive deletes. Pushes, tag creation, gh pr create/merge and gh release are blocked until the project approves them in its CLAUDE.md. Read-only commands such as git status, git log or gh pr view remain allowed; a session-start hook that gives Claude the plan and the rules to re-read; a watcher that notices when the rules in a project have changed during a session or differ from the template. Install it once per machine: claude plugin marketplace add AngeloDotNet/claude-config claude plugin install kit-config@claude-config The current version is 1.8.0. Using it in a project The documentation covers three situations: New project: copy the rules and the CLAUDE.md template, fill in the project fields, then ask Claude to start the project. Existing project without rules: use the "Git only" mode, which keeps only the core and git modules and leaves the existing code alone. Existing project with rules: bring the rules up to the latest template version. The CLAUDE.md in each project holds only what is specific to that project. Choices such as architecture, ORM, database, multi-tenancy or the ASVS level are never assumed: the template asks for them and they are recorded once. The copia-regole.bat script copies the rules and root files into a project folder and can update the rules already present. Caveats This is my own opinionated setup, not a universal standard. Some details are not yet verified against their sources, and the changelog says so openly. For example, the exact PostgreSQL row-level security syntax and passkey support in ASP.NET Core Identity on .NET 10 are marked to be checked the first time they are used. Treat the rules as a starting point and adapt them to your projects. Links Documentation: http://docs-claude-config.aepserver.it/ License: MIT If you try it on a real project, I would like to hear what breaks first.

articles.title: Day 3 never came. My son and I stopped racing and built a game engine.
articles.description: In March, my son and I made a bet. 80 days. Build real software. Sell it. Father vs son, shipping every day. Day 2 ended with four words: Something has to change. Then the posts stopped. Here's why. The race stopped We'd been racing each other. Breadth against depth. Me knocking on more doors, him polishing one thing until it shone. Then we noticed something. We have different skills, and we think in different ways. What one of us lacks, the other brings. And we'd both been making games and game engines for years. Separately. So we stopped racing and started building together. Day 2 said we had to work smarter. This was it. Synergy turned out to be real. What we built Myth Engine. Myth Engine is a game engine for 2D and 3D games. The games you make can run on the web, on desktop and on mobile. It's built with JavaScript and Babylon.js, and it uses ECS (entity component system), which makes putting a game together feel intuitive and helps games run fast. You make games in the editor on Windows, with Visual Logic blocks, JavaScript, or both. The editor draws your level with the game's own runtime, so you see it as it will look in the game. And games to go with it We didn't just build the engine. We made games with it. 2D and 3D games, shooters, puzzles, platformers, worlds made of blocks and science labs, all made in Myth Engine. Inside the editor 2D Move, rotate and scale with the handles or the G, R and S keys. Split screen, minimaps and cameras that follow the player, with no code. Tile maps on square, isometric and hex grids. 3D Blender's axes and keys: Z is up, and G, R and S move, rotate and scale. Scenes built from sculpted terrain, grass, water and lights. Havok physics makes objects fall, collide and tumble. Objects built from components Every object is built from components that you add and tune. The same Object Editor builds 2D and 3D objects. Game rules: blocks, code, or both Game rules are Visual Logic blocks you connect: when something happens, such as a button press, do something. Build a behavior once and attach it to as many objects as you like. Pause the game right before any block runs, step through it, and watch each object's values change. JavaScript works instead of blocks or alongside them, with suggestions for your project's own objects and sounds as you type. JavaScript libraries can be added from a catalog, and they're bundled into your game. Pixel art Paint layered art directly into your game. Mirrored drawing, crisp pixel rotation and patterned gradients. Recolor a sprite by changing its palette. Looks and effects Ready-made looks, from old film and Game Boy to thermal camera and comic-book print. Up to four can be combined. Build new looks from connected blocks, or write them as code. Particle effects in 2D and 3D, starting from presets such as fire, rain and confetti. Worlds made of blocks Generated worlds with hills, caves, ores and trees, and a map preview before you play. Block worlds can be built by hand too. Sharing your game Web games export as a single file or a web folder. Desktop and mobile exports are projects you finish building yourself. Multiplayer is built in, with a lobby and a relay server you host. There's more in the full tour on itch.io: What Myth Engine can do. The new scoreboard Us Products Myth Engine, plus the games we've made with it Free guides Complete games, built step by step from an empty project One column now. That's the twist. Try it The free version has no time limit. Exporting finished games needs the full version, which is a one-time purchase with no royalties. Download the free version Play the games and find the free guides Come say hi on Discord Call this Day 3. It just took a little longer than a day. Next time: blocks or code? We settled it the family way.

articles.title: Quote and contract from the same numbers: a wedding vendor's spreadsheet + the 11 clauses that hold up
articles.description: Every wedding vendor I have talked to has the same story. Somewhere around booking number twenty, a client cancels six weeks out, asks for the deposit back, and the vendor realises the "contract" was a WhatsApp message that said "ok booked!". The second-most-common story is the quote that got sent as a photo of a notes app, with one line item missing, and the argument that followed on the wedding day. Both problems have the same fix: a quote and a contract that come from the same numbers. Here is the structure I use, with the spreadsheet logic that keeps the two in sync. Start with one settings sheet The mistake most vendors make is writing percentages in three places: the quote says "30% deposit", the contract says "40% second payment", and the payment reminder you send says something else. Put every rule in one place and let everything reference it: Setting Example Deposit (retainer) 30% Second payment 40%, due 30 days before Final balance = 100% − deposit − second Quote validity 14 days Reschedule fee 10% of contract Late fee 0.1% per day, capped at 5% The final-balance cell is a formula, not a number, so it can never fail to add up. A one-line check next to it (=IF(ROUND(dep+second+final,4)=1,"OK","CHECK")) catches the day you change the deposit and forget the rest. The quote: codes, not retyping A pricelist with a short code per item (PKG-03, ADD-06) means the quote sheet needs only two inputs per line: code and quantity. Name, unit and price come from a lookup: =IFERROR(INDEX(Pricelist!$C$5:$C$64, MATCH(A13, Pricelist!$A$5:$A$64, 0)), "CODE NOT FOUND") INDEX/MATCH rather than XLOOKUP because clients open your PDF, but you might open the sheet in Google Sheets, LibreOffice or an older Excel, and all of them evaluate this one. A COUNTIF on the code column flags duplicates before they bite. The totals block then reads Subtotal → Discount → Tax (only if a Yes/No setting says you collect it) → Total → Deposit to book → Remaining balance. The deposit line is =ROUND(Total * Setup! Deposit, 2) — the same cell the contract will quote. Due dates from the event date Payment schedules fail because due dates are typed by hand. Compute them: Second payment due = EventDate − Setup! DaysBeforeSecond Final balance due = EventDate − Setup! DaysBeforeFinal Status = IF(paid >= due_amount, "PAID", IF(TODAY() > due_date, "OVERDUE", IF(paid > 0, "PARTIAL", "DUE"))) Add a late-fee estimate that is capped (MIN(overdue × rate × days, overdue × 5%)). A fee without a cap looks predatory in a dispute; a capped one is the number a mediator will accept. The 11 clauses the contract needs The clause list that has held up for the vendors I have worked with, in order: Scope — the exact line items from the quote, by code, and a sentence saying anything not listed is not included. Date, venue, timeline — plus a deadline for the client's final run of show. This is the clause that saves you when "we moved the first dance" becomes "you missed the first dance". Fees and payment — the instalment table, the account, who pays transfer fees, and that the date is not reserved until the deposit lands. Cancellation and rescheduling — deposit non-refundable, one reschedule for a fee, new date within 12 months. Force majeure — obligations suspended, new date without a reschedule fee, sunk costs not refunded. Deliverables, delivery, revisions — counts, formats, turnaround in business days, number of revision rounds, and a deadline for the client to pick album photos. Copyright and portfolio use — copyright stays with you, client gets a personal-use licence, an explicit opt-out for social posting. Obligations of each side — crew meals, vendor passes, travel for destination events, your right to substitute crew. Liability cap — total liability limited to what was paid. Standard in creative services. Dispute resolution and governing law — negotiation first, then your local courts or mediation. General — amendments in writing (email counts), e-signatures valid, exhibits listed. Then a one-page delivery and acceptance record. The signature on it starts the revision clock, which closes the "I only just looked at the gallery" conversation nine months later. One habit that matters more than the template Walk the client through the checklist before sending the contract. Twenty clauses, two minutes on a call or a voice note. Clients sign faster when nothing in the document surprises them, and the vendors who do this report almost no disputes — not because the contract is tougher, but because expectations were set when everyone was still happy. If you would rather not build this yourself, I packaged the workbook (7 sheets, 450+ formulas, zero macros) and the 11-section agreement as the Wedding Vendor Contract & Quotation Pack 2026 — English edition ($14, Excel + Word, works in Google Sheets/Docs). There is also an Indonesian-language edition with local tax and stamp-duty wording.

articles.title: I shipped my extension in 9 languages to two stores. Here's what broke.
articles.description: I shipped the same extension update to the Microsoft Edge Add-ons store and the Chrome Web Store in nine languages last week. The code change was maybe forty lines. The listing work took two days and broke in three different ways. If you're about to localize a browser extension, here's what the consoles do not warn you about. Why bother localizing at all When you have no audience, store search is the only distribution channel you get for free. A monolingual listing only competes in English — the most crowded query space in both stores. A localized listing competes in a much thinner pool, because most indie extensions never translate anything. That's the whole argument. It is not about "global reach". It's about being one of four results instead of one of four hundred. Gotcha 1: every locale has its own character limit, and one of them is brutal In Edge Add-ons, the short description stored in your manifest (extDescription) is capped at 132 characters — per locale, and it's a hard package-level validation, not a warning. I had five of nine locales over the limit and did not find out until the upload refused the package. German and Russian blew past it almost immediately, because the same sentence is simply longer in those languages. "Summarize any page with your own AI key" is 41 characters in English and comfortably over budget once translated with any precision. The fix is unglamorous: write the translation, then cut it to fit, then accept that the German short description is going to be a slightly different sentence than the English one. Don't translate; rewrite for the constraint. The long description has a floor as well as a ceiling — 250 to 2000 characters. A too-short translation fails validation just like a too-long one, which is easy to hit in languages where you are being terse. Gotcha 2: search terms are a budget, not a field Edge gives you up to 7 search terms per language, and caps you at 21 unique terms across the whole listing. Not 21 per language — 21 total, deduplicated across all nine. That means the term you use in English ("cookie banner") and the term you use in German ("Cookie-Banner") count separately, but repeating "cookie" in six languages does not give you six shots at it. Two of my listings blew the global budget — 23 and 22 terms — because I had been treating each language as an independent listing. Plan the term set once, in a spreadsheet, before you touch the console. The console will let you type the eighth term and only complain at submit time. Gotcha 3: the language dropdown is asynchronous and it will silently eat your work This one cost me an entire product's listing. In the Chrome Web Store dev console, the "edit language" control is a custom dropdown that loads its options asynchronously. If you switch language and start typing into the description field within a second or two, you are still writing into the previous language's field. Nothing visually indicates this. The field looks empty because it re-renders, and your input lands wherever the model currently points. The result: every locale ended up holding the text of its neighbour. English field held German, German held Russian, and so on down the list. The store accepted it without complaint, because each field was a valid description of the right length. Two rules came out of that: After switching, poll the page until the visible "currently editing language" indicator actually names the language you asked for. Do not rely on a fixed sleep. Verify by reading the saved text back, per locale, with a page refresh between switches. One page load can reliably switch language once; a second switch in the same load is where it goes wrong. Read-back verification is the only thing that caught this. A screenshot would not have. Gotcha 4: naming other companies' products gets you rejected for keyword spam My first submission was rejected by an automated check within ten minutes. The cause was a sentence in the description listing the consent-management platforms the extension supports — eight third-party trademarks in a row. To a human that reads as a feature list. To the automated reviewer it reads as keyword stuffing. I rewrote it as a capability statement — what the extension does to a banner, not whose banner it is — and it went through. The same wording problem had already burned me once on a different product and a different store, so this is a pattern, not bad luck: Describe what your software does. Do not enumerate other companies' names to prove coverage. Gotcha 5: in Edge, editing the Properties page saves a draft and nothing else The Partner Center has a page where you can edit your listing properties. Editing there and hitting save does not publish anything. The change sits as a draft until you walk the full update flow — Properties, then Privacy, then Listings, then Publish, then Submit — and the certification notes field must be filled or the submit is blocked. Also, re-rendering between steps clears fields you already filled. In my case the certification notes textarea was wiped by clicking a radio button after typing. Fill the free-text explanation last. The verification loop that actually works After all of that, the process I'd keep is: Precheck locally. Character counts, term counts, and a scan for third-party brand names — all checkable before upload, none checkable after rejection. Fill one language at a time, confirming the active language before typing. Read back every field, refreshing between languages, and diff against your source text. Publish last, and treat any field with free text as something that may be cleared by the next click. None of this is interesting engineering. It's just the difference between shipping in two days and shipping in two weeks. I build small, privacy-first browser extensions — everything runs locally, and when an AI feature needs a model you bring your own key. If the workflow above saved you a rejection, the extensions are at glenkit.com.
